pedagogy.summary: This is the procedural core of ratio notation: writing a relationship as a:b, simplifying it to its simplest form by dividing both parts by their highest common factor, and converting between a ratio and the fractions of the whole it implies (3:2 means 3/5 and 2/5). The work rests directly on factors/HCF and on the part-to-part vs part-to-whole distinction. Teaching should keep the notation tied to meaning — a:b is 'for every a there are b' — so that simplifying is understood as keeping the same relationship with smaller numbers (an equivalent ratio), and so that the leap to fractions correctly uses the WHOLE (a+b) as the denominator, not the other part.
bestPractices: Tie a:b to 'for every a there are b' and keep order fixed to the wording (boys:girls must be written boys-first) to prevent order reversal.

Teach simplifying as dividing BOTH parts by a common factor, and 'simplest form' as dividing by the highest common factor — explicitly check nothing divides both parts again (12:8 ÷4 = 3:2, and 3,2 share no factor).
Make equivalent ratios explicit: 12:8, 6:4, 3:2 all describe the same relationship — use a ratio table or scaled bars to show they are the same 'for every'.
Draw the part-to-whole conversion from a bar: 3:2 has 5 equal blocks, so 3/5 are the first part and 2/5 the second — the denominator is the total number of parts.
Handle decimal/fraction ratios by scaling up to whole numbers first (0.5:2 → 1:4; 1/2:1/3 → 3:2 via a common multiplier) before simplifying.
Contrast the ratio 3:2 with the fraction 3/2 aloud so children do not read a:b as a/b.
keyRepresentations: a:b notation anchored to 'for every a there are b'
Bar model of a+b equal blocks for the part-to-whole conversion (3:2 → 3/5, 2/5)
HCF/common-factor working shown beside the ratio (÷4)
Scaling-up step for decimal/fraction ratios (×2, ×10) to reach whole numbers
commonMisconceptions: Stops before simplest form — divides by a common factor but not the HCF (12:8 → 6:4 and leaves it)
Reverses the order relative to the wording (writes girls:boys)
Converts a:b to fractions using the other part as the denominator (3:2 → 3/2) instead of the whole (3/5)
Simplifies by subtracting a constant from both parts (12:8 → 4:0 or 11:7) rather than dividing — an additive slip

learn.summary: Teach ratio notation as meaning before manipulation: a:b means 'for every a there are b', with order fixed to the wording (boys:girls written boys-first). Simplify by dividing BOTH parts by a common factor, reaching simplest form only when no common factor other than 1 remains (equivalently, once the parts have been divided by their highest common factor). Convert to fractions of the whole using the TOTAL of the parts as the denominator (3:2 means 3/5 and 2/5, not 3/2). Handle decimal or fraction ratios by first scaling up to whole numbers. The core insight is that simplifying keeps the SAME relationship with smaller numbers (an equivalent ratio).

activities.title: Ratio simplifying bench with a shape-stays-the-same check
feedback: If a child stops at 6:4, the 'can this go smaller?' indicator stays red — prompt: 'Is there a number that divides BOTH again?' Both parts still share a factor of 2, so divide again to reach 3:2.
If a child reads 3:2 as 3/2, point to the snapped whole: count ALL the parts (3+2=5); the denominator is the total five blocks, so boys are 3/5.
If the scaled bars change shape after an operation, that operation did not preserve the relationship — check whether both parts were divided by the SAME factor (subtracting a constant does not work).
activities.rationale: Simplifying and converting are manipulations that this activity has learners perform directly — dividing both parts, seeing the relationship preserved, and reading off the part-to-whole fractions — with immediate feedback aimed at the 'not fully simplified' and 'wrong denominator' errors. The scaled bars and the green/red checker are intended to make the preserved relationship and the simplest-form end-state visible.
sourceClaims: A ratio a:b is a part-to-part comparison ('for every a there are b'); the part-to-whole fraction uses the total of the parts, which children conflate with the part-to-part relationship.

Using ratio notation including reduction to simplest form, and understanding that a multiplicative relationship can be expressed as a ratio or a fraction related to the arithmetic of fractions, is the required KS3 content (introduced informally at Year 6 with a:b notation).
learnerActions: Enter a ratio such as 12:8 and simplify it by repeatedly choosing a number to divide BOTH parts by (e.g. ÷4 straight to 3:2, or ÷2 to 6:4 then ÷2 again).
Watch two scaled bars drawn beside the numbers: as 12:8 becomes 6:4 becomes 3:2, the bars keep the same shape/proportion, showing the relationship is preserved.

Use a 'can this go smaller?' indicator that stays red while a common factor greater than 1 still divides both parts and turns green only when none does, so 'simplest form' becomes a testable end-state.
Then snap the 3 and 2 blocks together into one whole of 5 and read off the part-to-whole fractions 3/5 and 2/5 from the total number of blocks.
For a decimal or fraction ratio (0.5:2, or 1/2:1/3), first apply a scale-up step (×2, ×10, or a common multiplier) to reach whole numbers (0.5:2 → 1:4; 1/2:1/3 → 3:2), then simplify.
activities.intendedInsight: Simplifying a ratio keeps the same 'for every' relationship with smaller numbers; simplest form means no common factor remains; and converting to a fraction uses the whole (a+b) as the denominator.

activities.title: Scored practice set with targeted ratio errors
feedback: If 3/2 is chosen for the fraction of the whole, explain it compares the two parts, not part to whole; the denominator must be the total of the parts (5), so boys are 3/5.
If 2/5 is chosen for the fraction of the whole, note that 2/5 is the second part's share; the first part is 3 of the 5 equal parts in total, giving 3/5.
If 6:4 is left as the simplify answer, note both parts still divide by 2, so it is not yet simplest form.
If a match is wrong, check that both parts of the matched ratio divide down to the same pair of numbers (3 and 2).
activities.rationale: Writing, simplifying and converting ratios is well suited to a scored set with fill-in and matching items and incorrect options aimed at the exact misconceptions. This checks recognition and fluency after the meaning is established but does not itself elicit the full self-directed simplifying procedure, so it complements rather than replaces the manipulation activity.
learnerActions: Fill in the blanks to simplify: 12:8 = ☐:☐ (expecting 3:2 in simplest form).
Match several ratios (12:8, 6:4, 9:6) to their shared simplest form 3:2.

Choose what fraction of the whole the first part of 3:2 represents, from options including 3/5 (correct), 3/2 (the part-to-part comparison read as a fraction) and 2/5 (the other part's share of the whole).
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent writing, simplifying and converting of ratios, with the common errors made explicit through the wrong-answer options offered.

activities.title: Verbal coaching of the simplest-form check
feedback: If the child declares a ratio finished too early, ask again whether a single number divides both parts.
If the child subtracts, show that 12:8 → 4:0 removes one quantity entirely and no longer describes the same situation.
activities.rationale: Spoken coaching can rehearse the HCF check and the divide-not-subtract principle; because a symbolic-procedural skill needs repeated independent practice for fluency, this is intended to support the manipulation and practice activities rather than stand alone. The relative efficacy of coaching versus doing is a design judgement, not an established result.
learnerActions: Work through one ratio aloud with a prompt such as 'Can both numbers be divided again?' at each step until no common factor remains.
State why 4:0 (from subtracting) cannot be a valid simplification: it would mean 'no girls', which changes the relationship.
activities.intendedInsight: Simplest form is reached only when no factor divides both parts, and simplifying must preserve the 'for every' relationship (divide, do not subtract).

activities.title: Worked simplify-and-convert reference
feedback: Point back to the ÷4 step when a learner forgets that both parts share that factor.
Point back to the 5-part bar when a learner is unsure where the denominator 5 comes from.
activities.rationale: A fixed worked example shows one complete simplify-and-convert chain and serves as a reference; because it cannot be manipulated across many ratios it does not by itself build fluency, so it is intended for use alongside active practice.
learnerActions: Reveal, on a fixed example, that 12:8 divides by 4 to give 3:2.
Reveal on the bar for 3:2 that there are 5 equal parts, so the fractions of the whole are 3/5 and 2/5.
activities.intendedInsight: A single clear chain from a ratio to its simplest form and then to fractions of the whole, available as a reference model.

constraints: Keep order fixed to the wording: boys:girls must be written boys-first, to prevent order reversal.

Simplest form is reached once both parts have been divided by their highest common factor, either in one step or in several smaller steps; always check that no number other than 1 divides both parts again (e.g. 12:8 ÷4 = 3:2, and 3 and 2 share no common factor other than 1). Stopping at 6:4 is not simplest form.
The part-to-whole fraction uses the TOTAL of the parts as the denominator (3:2 → 3/5 and 2/5), never the other part (not 3/2).
Decimal or fraction ratios must first be scaled up to whole numbers (0.5:2 → 1:4; 1/2:1/3 → 3:2 via a common multiplier) before simplifying.
Contrast the ratio 3:2 with the fraction 3/2 aloud so a:b is not misread as a/b.
Simplifying must preserve the relationship by dividing, not subtracting: 12:8 → 4:0 or 11:7 is an additive error that changes the 'for every'.

The scored practice set checks recognition and fluency but does not elicit the full independent simplifying procedure; it complements active manipulation rather than replacing it. In a fraction-of-the-whole item, keep the incorrect options genuinely distinct in value (e.g. 3/2, the part-to-part reading, versus 2/5, the other part's share of the whole), not numerically equal forms of the same error.
The fixed worked example is a reference only; it cannot be manipulated across many cases and so does not build fluency by itself.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh retrieval or re-verification of the cited sources; activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source citations support the general principles (part-to-part vs part-to-whole; KS3/Year 6 curriculum placement) but do not establish the efficacy of any specific activity described here.

Comparative-efficacy framings (a symbolic skill 'better drilled by doing than by talking', or that a 3D treatment 'adds nothing') reflect design preference, not established comparative efficacy; retained only as narrowly scoped design notes, not universal laws.

On the original diagnostic counterexample '10:15 boys to girls': the original '5:7.5' is arithmetically correct (10÷2=5, 15÷2=7.5). The point is that halving does NOT reach an integer simplest form because 15 is odd; only dividing by the HCF (5) gives 2:3. Treated as a reasoning note, kept out of learner-facing text.

probeDeeper: 'Is 6:4 the same relationship as 3:2? How do you know?' — checks equivalent-ratio understanding behind simplifying.
'You wrote 3/5 are boys — where does the 5 come from?' — forces the whole-as-denominator to be justified.
Counterexample: 'A different class has ratio 10:15 boys to girls — simplify that' — a child with the HCF idea gives 2:3; a child who only halves gives 5:7.5 or stalls on the odd numbers.
'Could you write this ratio with even smaller whole numbers than your answer?' — tests whether they can confirm simplest form.
assess.correctAnswer: Ratio 12:8, simplified to 3:2 (dividing both by the HCF 4). Boys are 3 out of the 5 equal parts, so 3/5 of the class.

errorPatterns.pattern: Stops before simplest form: divides by a common factor but not the HCF (12:8 → 6:4 and leaves it), thinking it is simplified
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'is there a number that divides BOTH again?' and rebuild the highest-common-factor idea; check simplest form by confirming no common factor remains.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child writes 6:4 (or 12:8 ÷2) and moves on; both parts still share a factor of 2

errorPatterns.pattern: Converts the ratio to a fraction using the other part as the denominator: gives boys as 3/2 (out of the girls) instead of 3/5 (of the whole)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the bar: count ALL the parts in the whole class (3+2 = 5) to set the denominator; distinguish part-to-part (ratio) from part-to-whole (fraction).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child writes 3/2, or uses 2 or the un-simplified 8 as the denominator, not the total number of parts (5)

errorPatterns.pattern: Reverses the order: writes 8:12 / 2:3 for boys-to-girls, not matching the wording
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach ratio — scaffold careful mapping: underline the order in the question ('boys : girls') and write the parts in that order. A lapse, not a gap.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The ratio is correct in value but the parts are the wrong way round relative to 'boys to girls'

errorPatterns.pattern: Simplifies by subtracting rather than dividing (12:8 → 4:0, or takes a constant off both parts)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that 4:0 means 'no girls', which is false — simplifying must keep the same 'for every'. Rebuild simplifying as dividing both parts by the same factor.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child subtracts from both parts; the resulting 'ratio' no longer preserves the relationship

responseLevels.gap: Cannot write the ratio in the right order or simplify it; subtracts instead of divides, or gives a fraction with the wrong denominator and cannot correct it.
responseLevels.full: Writes the ratio in the correct order, simplifies to simplest form by the HCF, confirms no common factor remains, and converts correctly to fractions of the whole (a/(a+b)), transferring to new and awkward (decimal/fraction) ratios.
responseLevels.partial: Writes and partially simplifies the ratio (e.g. reaches 6:4) and can convert to a fraction for the practised case, but does not reliably reach simplest form or mishandles the part-to-whole denominator, or the method is fragile when numbers are awkward (odd, decimal).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: In a class there are 12 boys and 8 girls. Write the ratio of boys to girls, then simplify it as far as it will go. After that, tell me what fraction of the whole class are boys. Do it however you like — I'll watch, you don't need to explain the rule.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the work reveals the two hinge points: whether the child simplifies to the HIGHEST common factor (3:2) or stops early (6:4), and whether the fraction uses the WHOLE as the denominator (3/5) or the other part (3/2). A child with the procedure divides both parts by 4 and reads 3/5 off the five parts; a child without it leaves a shared factor, reverses the order, or gives 3/2 — each visible in the written work without being asked about it.
